summary: Discovery focused on per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer wants to understand unit economics for chat agents (avg 1.2k tokens per session), budget cap of ~$30k/month for inference, and whether dedicated capacity + KV caching will achieve required latency and cost targets.
topics: per-token pricing and effective cost after batching
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Liam our SE, we'll run through cost econ and tradeoffs.
[00:12] Raj: Hi, Raj here. Quick background, we run a customer support agent and a portfolio summarization agent, around 120k sessions a month, about 1.2k tokens per session on avg, so rough ballpark 144M tokens/month. We're trying to see where Redwood fits vs our in-house infra and the big APIs.
[00:28] Liam: Great, that's super helpful. Two quick Qs up front — what latency SLO are you targeting and do you have a hard budget?
[00:34] Sofia: Target is sub-400ms p50 for interactive chat in the UI, and budget is about 30k/mo for inference right now, but we can consider reserved commit if the math works.
[00:47] Maya: Okay, and are you leaning Hosted or would Private/dedicated be required for compliance?
[00:51] Raj: Currently Hosted is fine for prod but we're very interested in Dedicated for predictable throughput. Private is possible later for some regulated clients.
[01:02] Liam: Good. So cost levers at a high level: per-token list price (hosted), effective per-token after batching and KV / prefix caching, and then for Dedicated you can move to committed capacity which changes the unit cost calculus. Also quantization and model choice matter.
[01:20] Ethan: Can you explain the batching effect? We saw claims that batching helps throughput but increases tail latency.
[01:26] Liam: Yep. In Redwood Hosted our runtime does continuous batching — small windows to collect tokens across concurrent requests; for a throughput workload that helps drive down cost per token because GPU utilization improves. For interactive UI you can tune the batch window (we default to ~8-12ms) which keeps latency low but still gets some batching efficiency. For Dedicated you can configure bigger batch targets since you control pool sizing.
[01:45] Raj: And KV cache? We have a lot of repeated prefixes for our summary agent.
[01:49] Liam: KV / prefix caching cuts tokens by returning cached KV states for repeated prompts — in some workflows we've seen >40% token reduction when prompts share context. It's workload dependent. There's also embedding-level caching for rerank/lookup workloads.
[02:05] Sofia: How do we model this in pricing? We need a per-effective-token number to compare to our internal infra.
[02:11] Maya: We usually build a cost model. Base hosted rate is X per 1k tokens for generation + Y per 1k tokens for prompt tokens — (note: Maya says actual sheet will be emailed). But the effective cost = base_rate * (1 - cache_reduction) * (1 - batching_saving). For Dedicated, you take monthly commit and amortize fixed infra cost across tokens.
[02:31] Raj: Can you give example math?
[02:33] Liam: Sure. Say hosted list is $0.80 per 1k tokens (generation+prompt combined for the model you pick) — if your KV caching reduces tokens by 30% and batching/continuous improvements yield another 20% effective token saving, effective rate becomes 0.8 * 0.7 * 0.8 ≈ $0.448 per 1k effective tokens. For 144M tokens that is about $64.5k/month, so above your $30k target.
[02:59] Sofia: So how do we get under $30k?
[03:01] Liam: Options: 1) Dedicated where committed GPU pools drop marginal cost significantly — amortized commit could bring you down to roughly $0.15-$0.25 per 1k effective tokens depending on model/quant/usage; 2) change model to a cheaper open model we host or a quantized variant; 3) increase cache hit rate and more aggressive batching via Dedicated.
[03:23] Raj: I remember seeing numbers where Dedicated made sense at certain QPS thresholds. What's the break-even?
[03:28] Liam: For your traffic shape (avg session 1.2k tokens, 120k sessions) the break-even is around 80-120M tokens/month depending on model. You are in that ballpark so Dedicated is worth modeling. We'll run a dedicated vs hosted sensitivity.
[03:44] Ethan: On latency — can Dedicated keep 400ms p50?
[03:47] Liam: Yes — Dedicated can be tuned with target batch windows and isolation. Our customers get sub-300ms p50 for similar interactive agents. Tail latency depends on model size and sequence length but we've got grooming: smaller model variants, KV caching, and warm KV caches help.
[04:05] Sofia: Private deployment — does that change cost? We need VPC and KMS and some audit constraints for certain clients.
[04:11] Maya: Private adds platform and support fees and sometimes infra overhead if on-prem. For VPC in cloud we usually see a small premium on top of Dedicated. The big win is data residency and compliance. We'll provide a sketch in the pricing sheet.
[04:25] Raj: Security checklist — SOC2, SSO, audit logs?
[04:29] Maya: Yes SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS integrations, per-request audit logs for Private, and we can provide a security whitepaper link.
[04:38] Raj: Great. A couple more nitty gritty: do you charge for cached tokens returned from KV, and how do you count streaming tokens?
[04:46] Liam: We charge on output tokens generated + prompt tokens consumed as usual. For KV cache hits you only pay for tokens retrieved from backend when you have miss; full hits reduce both prompt and generation cost. For streaming, tokens are billed as generated; partial tokens from incremental stream are aggregated into final token count. There can be small discrepancies in transcripts vs billing but we provide token logs.
[05:06] Sofia: Regarding batching savings you quoted 20% — that's a guess?
[05:10] Liam: It's workload dependent. For interactive UI with many concurrent users, we've observed 10-25% cost reduction on hosted via quick batching. Dedicated with autoscale and larger pools can push that to 30-50% in some workloads. We'll include conservative and optimistic scenarios in the sheet.
[05:25] Raj: Can you run a benchmark with our real prompts? We can provide sample session traces.
[05:29] Maya: Yes — next step Liam will run a 48-hour benchmark on hosted and a Dedicated estimate; we'll need traffic profile and sample prompts from Ethan.
[05:38] Ethan: I'll export the last 7 days of session traces and share. Expect sequence lengths varying a lot — median 900 tokens, 95p 2.5k.
[05:47] Liam: That's helpful — 95p length will affect tail latency, and batching needs to handle a skewed length distribution. For Dedicated we can pin capacity and warm KV caches to reduce tail.
[06:00] Raj: Any gotchas on model versions and quantization? We use a custom instruction-tuned model right now in-house; can Redwood serve that?
[06:07] Maya: For private or dedicated we can host custom models; hosting custom weights for Hosted is limited but possible under enterprise agreements. Quantized variants usually cut memory and marginal cost. We'll include quantization fit notes in the doc.
[06:20] Sofia: What about rate limiting and burst capacity? During earnings calls we can see spikes.
[06:24] Liam: Dedicated supports burst pools and autoscaling policy. We can set a burst pool for brief surges; cost for bursts differs by policy but it's configurable.
[06:34] Raj: Ok this is helpful. Please send the pricing sheet and security docs; we'll reconvene after benchmark.
[06:40] Maya: Sounds good. I'll send pricing + a prefilled cost model where you can slot your cache % and batching assumptions. Liam will own the benchmark.
[06:48] Sofia: Thanks all.
[06:50] End call.

Notes on transcript quality: minor mis-hears — e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash, occasional dropped punctuation, and some speaker overlaps.
